A task is assigned to a team member who is absent from this meeting. The gold action item owner is that absent participant.

argv:
You generate synthetic meeting transcripts with gold annotations for LiveMinutes, a research dataset modeled on the AMI Meeting Corpus scenario meetings.

In AMI scenario meetings, a team of four plays a design team in a fictional company. The roles are Project Manager (PM), Marketing Expert (ME), User Interface designer (UI) and Industrial Designer (ID). A series has four meetings: (a) kickoff, (b) functional design, (c) conceptual design, (d) detailed design. Later meetings refer back to earlier ones.

Write natural spoken conversation the way AMI transcripts read: short turns, fillers ("um", "uh", "yeah"), backchannels ("mm-hmm", "okay"), interruptions, people building on each other, and some disfluency. Do not write a screenplay. Do not narrate. No stage directions.

Each segment is one dialogue-act-like unit: one speaker, usually one clause or short sentence, sometimes just a backchannel. Give each segment an AMI dialogue-act type from this set:
  bck backchannel, stl stall, fra fragment, inf inform, sug suggest, ass assess,
  el.inf elicit-inform, el.sug elicit-offer-or-suggestion, el.ass elicit-assessment,
  el.und elicit-comment-understanding, off offer, und comment-about-understanding,
  be.pos be-positive, be.neg be-negative, oth other

Absent participants NEVER speak. Speaker labels are ground truth: use only the labels you are given.

The gold annotations must be exactly true of the transcript you write. Refer to segments by their "n" number. Every number you cite must exist.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else: no prose, no markdown fences.

request.user:
Write meeting SY0204d: meeting "d" (detailed design) of series SY0204.

PROJECT
The team is designing a wearable step counter for seniors.

PARTICIPANTS (label, role, status for this meeting)
A  Marketing Expert (ME)  Priya  present
B  Industrial Designer (ID)  Tomasz  present
C  User Interface designer (UI)  Grace  ABSENT, never speaks
D  Project Manager (PM)  Martin  present

EARLIER MEETINGS IN THIS SERIES
Stay consistent with them. Refer back to them, follow up on their open action items, and keep the same product and team.

[SY0204a, kickoff]
  abstract: The project manager opened the kickoff meeting, and the marketing expert, industrial designer and user interface designer introduced themselves and their responsibilities. The project manager presented the project: a wearable step counter for seniors. Management has set a selling price of 30 euros, a maximum production cost of 12.50 euros per unit including the attachment, and a profit aim of 50 million euros on the international market. The team agreed that the device must be simple and have a big, high-contrast display. The wearing position (wrist, clip or pendant), fall detection and the battery type were discussed and left open. A task to research what seniors find readable was first given to the user interface designer and later moved to the marketing expert, who can use the marketing user panel. A family companion app was suggested but met objections on simplicity and cost. The need to check component costs was raised but nobody took it on.
  decisions: The step counter will have a big, high-contrast display.
  actions: The marketing expert will research readable font sizes and contrast for seniors using the marketing user panel. This task was reassigned from the user interface designer. The industrial designer will look into attachment options, comparing cost and sturdiness. The user interface designer will work on the interface functions, including the buttons and what the display shows. The project manager will send round the minutes. Checking the cost of components such as the sensor and screen was raised, but no owner was assigned.
  problems: The wearing position (wrist, belt or pocket clip, or pendant) has not been decided. Fall detection was proposed but not decided. Concerns are complexity and the 12.50 euro cost limit. Battery type (replaceable coin cell or rechargeable) is undecided. Competing basic pedometers sell for 10 to 15 euros. Component costs are unknown, and nobody is assigned to check them. The number of buttons is not settled.
  action item SY0204a.ai1: Research what seniors find readable (font sizes, contrast) by asking older people, using the marketing user panel (owner A, reassigned)
  action item SY0204a.ai2: Look into attachment options (wrist strap, clip, pendant) for cost and sturdiness (owner B, active)
  action item SY0204a.ai3: Work on the interface functions: which buttons and what the display shows (owner C, active)
  action item SY0204a.ai4: Check what the components (sensor, screen) actually cost (owner no owner, active)
  action item SY0204a.ai5: Send round the minutes of the meeting (owner D, active)
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer suggested wearing it as a belt or pocket clip or as a pendant. The wearing position was left open.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer proposed fall detection. It was not decided because of complexity and cost concerns.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert proposed a replaceable coin-cell battery instead of a rechargeable one. It was not decided.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The project manager suggested a maximum of two buttons. It was not settled.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert proposed a family companion app. The user interface designer and industrial designer objected on simplicity and cost.
  fact (plan_change): The readability research was first given to the user interface designer and then reassigned to the marketing expert.

[SY0204b, functional design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the functional design meeting, noted that the industrial designer was absent through illness, and recapped the kickoff decision on a big, high-contrast display. The marketing expert presented the user panel's readability findings: digits at least 1.5 centimetres tall, black on white preferred, and most seniors preferring a belt or pocket clip to a wrist strap. The user interface designer proposed a single large button that cycles between steps today, the time and yesterday's steps, with an automatic reset at midnight. The team accepted this. Fall detection was dropped for cost and complexity reasons. A vibration goal alert was proposed and left pending panel feedback and costs. The battery question was handed to the absent industrial designer. The open task of checking component costs was offered by the user interface designer but taken by the marketing expert, who already has supplier price lists.
  decisions: The device will be worn on a clip (belt or pocket), pending the industrial designer's sturdiness and cost check. The display will be black on white, with step-count digits at least 1.5 centimetres tall. The device will have one large button that cycles between steps today, the time and yesterday's steps. Holding it down enters time-setting mode. The step count will reset automatically at midnight. Fall detection will not be included in this product.
  actions: The marketing expert will check component costs: sensor, screen, button, clip and, if possible, a vibration motor. The marketing expert will ask the user panel whether seniors want a vibration alert when the daily goal is reached. The industrial designer (absent) will compare coin-cell and rechargeable batteries for size, cost and ease of changing within the clip housing. The industrial designer (absent) will check that the clip attachment is sturdy enough and within budget. The user interface designer will make a mock-up of the three screens and the single button with the large digits. The user interface designer will send the marketing expert information on screen sizes for pricing. The project manager will email the industrial designer with the decisions and his tasks, and will send round the minutes.
  problems: Battery type (coin cell or rechargeable) is still undecided. Coin cells are disliked for being hard to change, and recharging is disliked by the panel. The vibration goal alert is undecided because of component cost and battery drain. Component costs are still unknown. The marketing expert still sees sales potential in a family app, but it was rejected for this version.
  action item SY0204b.ai1: Check what the components cost (sensor, screen, button, clip and, if possible, vibration motor) using marketing's supplier price lists (owner A, active)
  action item SY0204b.ai2: Compare coin-cell and rechargeable batteries for size, cost and ease of changing in the clip housing (owner B, active)
  action item SY0204b.ai3: Check that the clip attachment is sturdy enough and within budget (continuing the attachment comparison from the kickoff) (owner B, active)
  action item SY0204b.ai4: Ask the user panel whether seniors would want a vibration alert when the daily goal is reached (owner A, active)
  action item SY0204b.ai5: Make a mock-up of the three screens and the single button with the large digits (owner C, active)
  action item SY0204b.ai6: Send the marketing expert information on screen sizes so she knows which screen to price (owner C, active)
  action item SY0204b.ai7: Email the industrial designer with the meeting's decisions and his tasks (owner D, active)
  action item SY0204b.ai8: Send round the minutes of the meeting (owner D, active)
  fact (absence): The industrial designer (Tomasz) was absent from the meeting because he was off sick.
  fact (plan_change): The project manager's kickoff suggestion of a maximum of two buttons was replaced by a decision to have only one button.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer proposed a vibration alert when the daily goal is reached. The project manager raised cost and battery concerns, and it was left pending panel feedback and costs.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert again suggested a family app would sell. The project manager and user interface designer rejected it for this version.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert again proposed a coin-cell battery. The user interface designer objected that coin cells are hard to change, and the question was handed to the industrial designer.

[SY0204c, conceptual design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the conceptual design meeting, welcomed the industrial designer back after his illness, and confirmed that the minutes and the email with the previous meeting's decisions had gone round. The marketing expert reported component costs from the supplier price lists: about 10.30 euros in parts without a vibration motor and 11.20 euros with one, excluding the battery, assembly and packaging. The user panel's response to a vibration goal alert was mixed, so the team dropped the vibration motor and chose a star icon on the display when a fixed daily goal of 5000 steps is reached. The industrial designer presented his battery and clip comparisons, and the team chose a coin-cell battery behind a large twist-off cap and a spring-steel clip. The user interface designer presented a mock-up of the three screens with 1.8 centimetre digits, which the marketing expert will test with the user panel.
  decisions: The vibration goal alert is dropped. No vibration motor will be included. A star icon will appear on the steps screen when the daily goal is reached. The daily goal is fixed at 5000 steps and cannot be set by the user. The device will use a CR2032 coin-cell battery behind a twist-off cap about 3 centimetres across, with a ridged edge and no screws. The device will use a spring-steel clip.
  actions: The marketing expert will take the mock-up to the user panel to check whether it can be read at arm's length. The marketing expert will update the cost list for a device with no motor, a coin cell and a steel clip. The industrial designer will make a model of the housing with the clip and the twist-off battery cap. The user interface designer will finish the screen layout, including the star icon. The project manager will send round the minutes. Checking what assembly and packaging add to the cost was raised twice, but no owner was assigned.
  problems: Assembly and packaging costs are unknown, and nobody is assigned to check them. The parts alone cost about 10.30 euros, which leaves little margin under the 12.50 euro limit. The industrial designer's safety cord loop was left open until the total cost is known. The marketing expert again raised the family app, but it remains rejected for this version.
  action item SY0204c.ai1: Find out what assembly and packaging add on top of the parts cost (owner no owner, active)
  action item SY0204c.ai2: Check whether a vibration motor fits in the clip housing next to the battery (owner B, dropped)
  action item SY0204c.ai3: Take the screen mock-up to the user panel to check whether it can be read at arm's length (owner A, active)
  action item SY0204c.ai4: Make a model of the housing with the clip and the twist-off battery cap (owner B, active)
  action item SY0204c.ai5: Finish the screen layout, including the star icon (owner C, active)
  action item SY0204c.ai6: Update the cost list for no motor, a coin cell and a steel clip (owner A, active)
  action item SY0204c.ai7: Send round the minutes of the meeting (owner D, active)
  fact (plan_change): The vibration goal alert, left pending at the functional design meeting, was dropped and replaced by an on-screen star icon.
  fact (plan_change): The user interface designer had objected that coin cells are hard to change, but she accepted a coin cell once the industrial designer proposed a large twist-off cap.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert again suggested a family app so that family members could set the goal. The user interface designer and project manager rejected it for this version.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer proposed a loop for a safety cord on the clip. The marketing expert liked it, but the project manager left it open until the total cost is known.
  fact (action_item_removed): The industrial designer's task to check whether the vibration motor fits was dropped after the motor was removed from the design.

EDGE CASES THIS MEETING MUST CONTAIN
Weave each one naturally into the project discussion. Each must be clearly present, and each must be tagged with the segments where it happens.
- F2_OFFERED_TAKEN_BY_OTHER [F2]: One person offers to do a task ("I could look into ..."), but a different person ends up taking it. The gold owner is the person who took it, and the history records the offer and the acceptance.
  Required gold labels: action_items, edge_cases.
- F2_TASK_TO_ABSENT [F2]: A task is assigned to a team member who is absent from this meeting. The gold action item owner is that absent participant.
  Required gold labels: action_items, edge_cases.

LENGTH
Between 90 and 140 segments.

GOLD LABELS
- summary: AMI-style abstractive summary in third person, using role names ("The project manager ..."). Sections: abstract (3-6 sentences), actions, decisions, problems (open issues). It reflects the meeting's FINAL state: corrected values, final plans, and no jokes or tangents reported as content.
- action_items: every task arising in the meeting. owner is the speaker label of the FINAL owner, and may be an absent participant. owner is null ONLY for a task nobody takes, with owner_unclear true. status is the final status: active, reassigned (owner changed; previous_owners lists earlier owners) or dropped. history lists the events in order. evidence_segments lists the supporting segments.
- qa_facts: atomic facts someone could later ask about ("Who was asked to ...?", "Did the team agree on ...?"). Include every decision (agreed true), every proposal nobody agreed to (type unagreed_proposal, agreed false), action items, removed action items, absences, and plan changes. Because this meeting follows earlier ones, include at least one fact of type reference_to_prior_meeting, with refers_to_meeting set, at a point where someone refers back to an earlier meeting. Do NOT write questions.
- edge_cases: one entry per edge case above, with its scenario_id and the segment numbers that contain it.

OUTPUT JSON SHAPE
{
  "segments": [{"n": 1, "speaker": "A", "da_type": "inf", "text": "..."}],
  "summary": {"abstract": ["..."], "actions": ["..."], "decisions": ["..."], "problems": ["..."]},
  "action_items": [{"n": 1, "description": "...", "owner": "C", "owner_unclear": false, "status": "active", "previous_owners": [], "history": [{"segment": 12, "event": "assigned", "by": "A", "owner": "C"}], "evidence_segments": [12, 13]}],
  "qa_facts": [{"type": "decision", "fact": "...", "agreed": true, "related_action_item": null, "refers_to_meeting": null, "evidence_segments": [40]}],
  "edge_cases": [{"scenario_id": "...", "segments": [20, 21, 22], "note": "one line on how it appears"}]
}
history events: proposed, offered, assigned, accepted, reassigned, dropped, restated. qa_facts types: decision, unagreed_proposal, action_item, action_item_removed, absence, plan_change, reference_to_prior_meeting, other. related_action_item is an action item's "n" or null. refers_to_meeting is an earlier meeting ID of this series or null.
